content: Calcium bicarbonate, also known as calcium hydrogen carbonate, is not a solid compound that can be isolated in its pure form. Instead, it exists only in aqueous solutions where calcium ions (Ca²⁺), dissolved carbon dioxide (CO₂), bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻), and carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) are present. The relative concentrations of these carbon-containing species are influenced by the pH of the solution. Bicarbonate ions are most prevalent in water with a pH range of approximately 6.36 to 10.25. Natural waters, such as those from streams, lakes, and wells, absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. As these waters interact with rocks and sediments, they acquire metal ions, primarily calcium and magnesium. Consequently, most natural waters can be considered dilute solutions of bicarbonates. These hard waters often lead to the formation of carbonate scale in pipes and boilers. Additionally, they react with soaps to produce an undesirable scum. Attempts to isolate calcium bicarbonate as a solid by evaporating its solution result in the decomposition of the bicarbonate into calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), water (H₂O), and carbon dioxide (CO₂). The reaction can be represented as follows: Ca(HCO₃)₂ (aqueous) → CO₂ (gas) + H₂O (liquid) + CaCO₃ (solid). This reaction is significant in the natural processes that form stalactites, stalagmites, columns, and other speleothems in caves. When water containing dissolved carbon dioxide (including additional CO₂ from soil organisms) passes through limestone or other calcium carbonate-rich minerals, it dissolves some of the calcium carbonate, enriching the water with bicarbonate ions. As this groundwater enters a cave, the excess carbon dioxide is released from the solution, leading to the precipitation of calcium carbonate, which is less soluble. This process not only contributes to the formation of cave structures but also plays a role in the development of the caves themselves.
